hero.lead: I build software from the interface down to the system it runs on. I like the part where it has to actually work.

about.label: About
about.title: I like turning things that don't work into things that do.
paragraphs: Usually that means software. Something is unclear, slow, or broken, and I want to understand it before I start changing it.
I like the whole path, not only the framework in front of me. The screen someone uses, the API behind it, and the machine it runs on are one problem.
Away from the computer I am often in the workshop, taking something mechanical apart, or playing drums. I like both. They are a good reminder that not every problem lives in a text editor.

skills.intro: I would rather understand a tool than collect them. These are the ones I use.

bluenordix-lead.summary: I lead development and still build with the team. The day-to-day is technical direction, architecture, and quality: keeping the codebase and the systems maintainable, rather than managing from a distance.

bluenordix-apprentice.summary: My apprenticeship, on production software with a small team. I worked across the stack and took on significant parts of the product. It was hands-on development during vocational training, not a stretch of ordinary full-time employment.

personal-portfolio.name: Personal Portfolio
personal-portfolio.summary: A portfolio website that is also a software project — designed and built from scratch.
personal-portfolio.imageAlt: The portfolio homepage, with the name Kevin Møller Madsen and two actions.
personal-portfolio.sourceNote: The source is public on GitHub, for anyone who wants to see how the portfolio is built.
overview: This is my personal portfolio. I designed and built it as a custom Angular application, with a Laravel backend, in a monorepo.
It presents my work, experience, skills, and background. It is also a software project in its own right: the same one you are looking at.
I did not want an online CV and nothing else. The portfolio is a chance to show how I approach a product: the interface, the structure, and the problems along the way.

role.detail: I designed and built the interface, from the page structure to the type and the feature components.
Laravel lives in the same repository. I run it locally with DDEV. The pages do not call it yet.
The layout reads typed data through one service, so the pages are not tied to the files that hold the content today.

paragraphs: The repository has two applications side by side. Frontend/ is the Angular site. Backend/ is Laravel.
Feature components read that service. It is the place an API can take over later.
architecture.diagram:
portfolio/
├── Frontend/    Angular application
└── Backend/     Laravel application

decisions.title: Angular and TypeScript
decisions.body: Standalone components, grouped by feature.

decisions.title: Laravel and DDEV
decisions.body: The backend is PHP, developed locally with DDEV.

decisions.title: One repository
decisions.body: Frontend and Backend sit next to each other.

decisions.title: A portfolio service
decisions.body: Templates read the service. The copy and the records sit behind it, not inside the layout.

decisions.title: Fluid layout
decisions.body: Type and spacing grow with the screen, then stop, so a large display does not turn the page into a billboard.

decisions.title: A quiet interface
decisions.body: Near-black, with deep navy in it. Motion is an entrance and a hover, then it stops.

challenges.problem: The page had to stay comfortable on a phone, fit a 1080p display, and still not look like a narrow column on a much larger screen.
challenges.approach: Sizes are fluid up to a point, and the reading column has a maximum width. Past that, the page stops growing.

challenges.problem: The first navigation highlight followed how much of a section was on screen. A tall section could stay active after the reader had moved on.
challenges.approach: The active item is now the last section that has passed a line just under the header.

result: The site is what I use to present the work. Building it is part of what it demonstrates.
This page is the template for the other projects, once they are written up.

mc-profile.name: MC Profile
mc-profile.summary: A Chrome extension that shows how old a Minecraft account is. Mojang and Microsoft do not show that themselves.
mc-profile.imageAlt: MC Profile listing, with the popup over a Minecraft landscape.
mc-profile.sourceNote: Published on the Chrome Web Store.
overview: It started in a conversation. We wanted to know how long we had had our Minecraft accounts, but Mojang and Microsoft do not show that. I found that one API call on Mojang's site already returns the value.

MC Profile is the extension I built from that. It opens as a popup and shows the account that is already signed in: when it was created, how old it is, how old the username is, the skin, the capes, and the UUID.
It reads the existing session. It does not ask for a password, and it does not ask for an account of its own. It is unofficial, and it is not affiliated with Mojang or Microsoft.

role.detail: I designed the popup so the account can be read at a glance.
I built it to use the Minecraft session that is already signed in, instead of a new login.

paragraphs: The extension is a popup. It reads the Minecraft session that is already signed in, and it does not ask for a password or a separate account.
Account age comes from one API call Mojang's site already makes. The other details are cached on the machine, so opening the popup again does not repeat the same requests.

decisions.title: The call Mojang's site already makes
decisions.body: The account pages do not show how old the account is. One request on Mojang's site returns that value, so the extension uses it.

decisions.title: A Chrome extension
decisions.body: It lives in the browser, so there is no separate site to sign in to.

decisions.title: The session that is already there
decisions.body: It reads the Minecraft session. The password is never typed into the extension.

decisions.title: A local cache
decisions.body: Details are kept on the machine, so the same requests are not sent every time the popup opens.

decisions.title: One popup
decisions.body: Creation date, age, username, skin, capes, UUID, and OG status sit in the same view.

challenges.problem: Mojang and Microsoft do not let you see how old your account is.
challenges.approach: One API call that Mojang's site already makes returns that value. The extension reads it from the session that is already signed in.

result: It is published on the Chrome Web Store.

danish-banknote-system.name: DanishBanknoteSystem
danish-banknote-system.summary: A system for my Danish banknote collection: what I own, what I want, and what the collection is worth.
danish-banknote-system.imageAlt: Seddelkatalog overview, with collection progress, grades, and an estimated value.
danish-banknote-system.sourceNote: The source is public on GitHub.
overview: I collect Danish banknotes, and I wanted one place to keep track of them. DanishBanknoteSystem is that system. In the app it is called Seddelkatalog.
It shows what I have, a wishlist, and statistics on what the collection is worth. The notes, prices, and grades come from the catalog at seddelkataloget.dk.
That catalog is a PDF. I ran it through an online OCR engine and used the result for the prices, the grades, and the rest of the catalog data.

role.detail: I shaped it around my own collection: the notes I own, a wishlist, and a value.
I built the Angular interface and the Laravel backend that hold the catalog and the collection.

paragraphs: The repository is a Laravel application, with an Angular frontend in frontend/. I run it locally with DDEV.
The catalog data, prices and grades included, comes from the Seddelkataloget PDF, read with an online OCR engine. The collection and the wishlist sit on top of that catalog.

decisions.title: The catalog, not a blank list
decisions.body: The notes, prices, and grades come from Seddelkataloget, so the collection is measured against the real catalog.

decisions.title: OCR, instead of typing the PDF
decisions.body: The catalog is a PDF. An online OCR engine pulled out the prices, the grades, and the other fields.

decisions.title: Collection, wishlist, and value together
decisions.body: The overview shows progress, the mix of grades, and an estimated value. Search is where a note is added to the collection or the wishlist.

decisions.title: What I paid, and what the catalog says
decisions.body: The collection can store a purchase price. The wishlist and the note page show the catalog price for each grade.

challenges.problem: The catalog I wanted to use is a PDF, not a database.
challenges.approach: I extracted the prices, grades, and the rest of the entries with an online OCR engine, and loaded that into the system.

result: I use it for my own collection: what I own, what I want, and an estimated value based on the catalog.
The source is public on GitHub.

elunio.name: Elunio
elunio.summary: A private SaaS platform for service businesses. They build a quote calculator and place it on the website they already have.
elunio.imageAlt: The Elunio product page, with a lawn-care quote calculator and an estimated price.
overview: Elunio is a SaaS platform I am building on my own, for businesses that quote service work. The business builds a calculator. A customer on their website answers a few questions and gets an estimated price.

The builder is visual. A question can be a number, a short text, one choice, several choices, a dropdown, or yes or no. It can be required, and it can stay hidden until another answer makes it relevant. The price can be fixed, per unit, a percentage, a tier, or a formula.

A finished calculation is a quote request, not the final quote. The business reviews it, prepares the quote with line items, and the customer can accept it. Each business has its own workspace, so calculators, customers, and quotes stay with that business.

role.detail: I defined the path from a question on the customer's site to a quote the business can send.
I built the Angular interface, including the calculator editor and the preview of what the customer sees.
I built the Laravel API for calculators, pricing, quotes, and access scoped to a workspace.

paragraphs: The workspace is an Angular application. Laravel serves the API behind it. Signing in opens a workspace, and the calculators, customers, and quotes belong to that workspace.
A calculator is configuration. The questions, when they appear, and how the price is calculated are stored with it. Saving keeps a draft. Publishing replaces the version a customer sees.

decisions.title: Configuration, not a form per business
decisions.body: A new calculator is new data. It does not need its own page in the codebase.

decisions.title: Draft, then publish
decisions.body: The editor can change questions and prices without putting an unfinished calculator in front of customers.

decisions.title: An estimate, then a quote
decisions.body: The calculator returns an estimated price. The business still writes the quote, with line items, before the customer accepts it.

decisions.title: One workspace per business
decisions.body: Access is scoped to the workspace. Another company's calculators and quotes are kept apart.

decisions.title: Billing is still being built
decisions.body: The billing screen has Free and Pro, and Agency is part of the plan. Stripe is under development. WordPress and Shopify embeds are planned.

challenges.problem: A price is rarely one number.
challenges.approach: A job can mix a fixed fee, a price per unit, a percentage, and a tier. The price has to follow the answers, including questions the customer never reached.

challenges.problem: A question that should not appear yet.
challenges.approach: Later questions depend on earlier answers. A hidden question cannot change the price.

challenges.problem: More than one business, one product.
challenges.approach: Each workspace keeps its own calculators, customers, and quotes. A person only sees the workspace they belong to.

result: A workspace can build a calculator, set the pricing, preview the customer view, and publish it.
Quote requests come back into the workspace, and a request can move from new to closed.
It is not in production. Stripe billing is still being built. WordPress and Shopify are planned.
